speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head L of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I stand up to speak in this House, I am often raising questions or asking the Ministry for things.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This time, I am standing to thank the Ministry for the phenomenal job it has done on our climate policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, I still have questions and many more things to ask for, but those will come later.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have shown tremendous leadership on the global stage at the 28th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP28) on climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We co-facilitated ministerial consultations on climate mitigation and co-chaired the First Global Stocktake of the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also taking steps to strengthen our climate resilience by looking into coastal protection, heat stress and updating our climate projects through the Third National Climate Change Study (V3).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have made our living environment safer and more livable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We introduced the statutory presumption for littering from flats, looked into preventing disease outbreaks and made our hawker centres more vibrant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have also made sure that our food and water supplies are resilient to safeguard against future crises.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2024, we are one more year closer to the 2030 deadline in the Singapore Green Plan 2030 and the 2050 deadline to reach net-zero emissions here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we are acting fast and taking bold steps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad the voices of many in this House and outside of this House have been heard and the Government has been taking concrete steps to look into what we have called for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Well, with the exception of secondhand smoke, for which we must do so much more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know my Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) colleagues, fellow MPs and I will be asking lots more questions about the Ministry's plans for 2024.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to a robust and lively debate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 has set concrete targets to reduce our carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is a whole-of-nation effort involving all stakeholders – Government agencies, enterprises, communities and individuals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Other targets, such as producing 30% of Singapore's nutritional needs locally and completing the formulation of coastal protection plans by 2030, are for the longer term.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) share an update on the progress made by Government agencies towards their 2030 Green Plan targets?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What had been the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and supply and logistics challenges caused by global political tensions and conflicts?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What about the progress among multinational corporations (MNCs) and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in terms of their environment, social and governance (ESG) performance?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, three years ago on 10 February 2021, we embarked on a bold journey with the Singapore Green Plan 2030, aiming to transform our nation into a sustainable and climate resilient future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Since then, the world has witnessed unprecedented climate challenges, and the urgency of our actions has only intensified.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Green Plan is a whole-of-nation movement that seeks to chart Singapore's green target over the next decade.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It strengthens Singapore's commitment under the United Nations (UN) 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda and the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The ultimate goal is to position Singapore to achieve its long-term net-zero emission aspiration by 2050.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Now, 1,110 days or 36 months on after the announcement of the Green Plan, what have we achieved?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There were five key targets listed in the Green Plan.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many trees have we planted out of our one million target?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Did the Government take into account how many trees were cut down to make way for development during the last three years as well?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For the trees that were removed, how many were matured trees that are more than a decade old?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am concerned that the replacement of these matured trees with young saplings may be contrary to our first target.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Biodiversity conservation needs further focus, ensuring our ecological wealth thrives along with urbanisation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Solar energy deployment has seen commendable upward trajectory with more solar panels deployed on Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats, commercial as well as industrial buildings, including our airport.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last year during the Budget, I suggested to make solar panel deployment mandatory for all new buildings so that we can hardwire this requirement into our building code.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, this will speed up our solar energy deployment as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are only one year away from 2025.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Once we have achieved this target, what is the next target?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: More Government incentives in subsidy, grants and tax benefit can be considered to encourage solar power adoption.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With more economic activities resuming to pre-COVID-19 levels, more waste will be generated.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many more tonnes of waste were sent to landfills annually over the last three years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will there be a review and a revision of this target in view of renewed economic activity?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Target number four is to make at least 20% of schools carbon neutral by 2030, encouraging sustainable practices in educational institutions and educating our young.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What are the challenges to achieve this target?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The weather is getting warmer and the schools are using more air-conditioning to provide a good, conducive and comfortable learning environment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Schools are also using more computer, AI as well as electronic devices that consumes more electricity.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What percentage of newly-registered cars now are classified as cleaner energy models today?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With more Certificates of Entitlement (COEs) released recently, there is certainly an increased number of cars on our roads.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: More cars mean more carbon emissions, as a majority of the cars do not belong to the cleaner energy models.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many EV chargers were installed in public car parks to cater for this transition over the last three years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are we bringing in new clean car models, including swappable batteries as well as cars running on hydrogen?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The strength of the Green Plan is the holistic approach involving multiple Ministries, and there are clear targets providing a roadmap for actions as well as the emphasis on renewable energy and waste reduction that aligns with global sustainability goals.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While the targets are ambitious, we could even aim higher.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For instance, exploring more aggressive renewable energy goals beyond quadrupling solar power deployment and other forms of renewable energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There should be more community engagement involving citizens, more actively through education, incentives and community-led initiatives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Invest in comprehensive public awareness campaigns to foster a culture of sustainability.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government should also establish robust mechanisms to track progress and hold stakeholders accountable and do timely reporting.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: More can be done to encourage collaborations with private sectors, research institutions, international partners to drive innovation and share best practices.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Green Plan should remain flexible to adapt to changing circumstances and emerging technologies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In summary, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 is a commendable step towards a greener and more sustainable future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By addressing the suggested areas for improvement, we can enhance its impact and ensure a resilient and thriving Singapore for generations to come.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Mr Chairman, with global warming, Singapore will not be spared.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Our days will become hotter, and we expect to have very hot days with temperatures exceeding 35 degrees Celsius.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: It has been projected that we will have more warm nights too, when temperatures exceed 26 degrees.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will MSE share its plans to help build our people's heat resilience and increase urban liveability in view of these rising temperatures?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will there be specific studies designed to better understand the impact of heat on vulnerable groups in our population and the appropriate measures to assist them?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will the Government utilise findings from our Third National Climate Change Study (V3) to strengthen our city's heat resilience and also to contribute to international climate science efforts?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ocean conservation and coastal protection are issues close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, MSE's GPC Chair Mr Louis Ng and I spoke up on an Adjournment Motion to emphasise the importance of safeguarding our oceans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that we continue fortifying our coasts to mitigate the impact of climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does the Ministry have to enhance local technical capabilities and citizen participation in this domain?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, are there initiatives to collaborate with IHLs to share data, analyse and further develop our expertise in coastal protection?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Increasing local agriculture and aquaculture production are key objectives in reaching our "30 by 30" goal.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must be cognisant of the environmental and natural wildlife as we tackle our food security challenges, as we are reshaping natural environments with development and technology.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, a study found that aquaculture activity in close proximity to coral reefs limits survivorship and growth rates.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand we are transforming the area into a high-tech agri-food zone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also important to support the livelihood of people impacted by this transition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the progress of the Lim Chu Kang Master Plan, including whether the Government will explore integrating offshore aquaculture sites and agriculture systems for more sustainable production and optimising the farming production zone?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And could the Minister also share the measures implemented by MSE to support local farmers who have been impacted by this transition?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Due to disruptions, El Niño risks and food export bans, various crops have risen in prices.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must increase our food resilience through minimising external disruptions and maximising internal production.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the progress of the Alliance for Action (AfA) for Local Produce Demand Offtake and Consumer Education and the SG Fresh Produce (SGFP) logo?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, I wish to request that MSE share with us a progress update on the Lim Chu Kang Masterplan.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Singapore Food Agency (SFA) had earlier said that a detailed Masterplan will be published by 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Care needs to be taken to create the conditions to help Lim Chu Kang become a successful agri-food cluster.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One question to consider is whether a clustering concept is suitable for agriculture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clustering works if there are true economies of scale, which may not exist if different farms at Lim Chu Kang choose to grow different produce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, vertical farms survive by differentiating their products for niche markets where prices are higher, but demand is also limited.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It would be difficult for vertical farms to compete on a large scale in Singapore, where most households would prefer cheaper produce imported from Malaysia and elsewhere, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Another stated objective of the Lim Chu Kang Masterplan is to create good jobs for Singaporeans, but finding locals who want to commute there may be a far greater challenge than we anticipate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, we could consider siting indoor farms in under-utilised buildings or residential areas.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's growing population of plant hobbyists is potentially a good source of farmhands, but long commutes could be a deal breaker for them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Returning to our food security goals, food security is about how we feed the masses during times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, to what extent will calorific efficiency be considered when SFA makes decisions about which crops should be grown under the Lim Chu Kang Masterplan?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is an important question because the high-end kale that a vertical farm needs to sell to be commercially viable is not nearly as valuable as sweet potatoes during a crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In essence, it is not clear to me how future tenants at Lim Chu Kang will balance commercial viability with food security objectives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, we need to have a larger conversation about how serious we are about ensuring food security by farming locally and what amounts of financial resources would be required to achieve this.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What has been the progress of our "30 by 30" plan?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Our agri-food producers face various issues, including lease durations, rising costs, lack of economies of scale and a challenging business environment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What measures are in place to ease these pressures and attract more producers and investors to this sector?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: And for a sustainable agri-food sector, we need strong support and demand from our consumers, too.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The AfA on Demand Offtake and Consumer Education was formed last February to look into demand and supply aggregation of local produce.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: One of its main objectives is to increase public awareness and also to build greater support for local produce through consumer education.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Also, how is the Government ensuring food security in view of the increasing frequency of food supply chain disruptions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What can Singapore consumers do to support our food resiliency?

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Mr Don Wee, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, I welcome MSE's inaugural GreenGov.SG report, which was released last December.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It shows how the public sector is progressing in its green transition journey, including its use of electricity and water, as well as in reducing its emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am sure all Singaporeans appreciate that the Ministry is being transparent and accountable to the public on its efforts to reduce its carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Decisions like prioritising the reduction of single-use items, such as bottled water for meetings and disposables for meals, as well as measures to replace potable water with non-potable water for irrigation, general washing and cooling, will have an impact beyond the public sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These actions are a positive influence for businesses and families who have yet to fully incorporate similar practices into their companies and lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The sources of emissions in the report refer to Scope 1 and 2 emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Direct emissions, such as those from waste burning as well as vehicles powered by internal combustion engines, fall under Scope 1.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The use of electricity is categorised under Scope 2 emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Scope 3 emissions, which refer to the indirect greenhouse gas (GHGs) emissions incurred as part of an organisation's value chain, like the emissions from purchased goods and services or business travel by employees, were not included in the report.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Scope 3 emissions may form a significant part of total emissions and may even exceed Scope 1 and 2 emissions combined.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government consider including Scope 3 emissions and other additional information, like waste data, in its next report?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As one of the biggest purchasers of goods and services, the public sector plays an important role in setting an example and leading the country to develop green habits, develop and use greener products, as well as adopt greener practices.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since 2007, the Government had put in sustainability requirements for selected goods and services, such as information and communications technology (ICT) equipment, electrical appliances, paper, water fittings, buildings and vehicles.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the Government's efforts to do even more to green its supply chain.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government will gradually introduce sustainability practices or requirements into procurement into more sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Chairman, let me begin by declaring that I am a senior executive with a large local enterprise and I manage the sustainability business and practices for the company, among other roles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In the FY2022 report, it mentioned that post-pandemic, an increase in activities is expected during the recovery, thus the GHG emissions in the near term will also increase.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I understand that we have been measuring and disclosing these emissions on Scope 1 and Scope 2.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, the Government is the largest procurement party for the public sector.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Can I ask what will the Government plan to include in the next GreenGov.SG report?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Furthermore, any GHGs reduction targets without Scope 3 may not be meaningful, since we do not have the visibility on the full supply chain, nor its materials at source or manufacturing processes to produce the products or services.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While I recognise it is difficult to grapple with Scope 3, the position that the Government takes in this respect will be a signal of what the industry, especially the corporates, should endeavour to achieve.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In our next phase of urbanisation and economic growth, many projects that we are undertaking from public housing, transport infrastructures to connectivity service provisions, the criteria that the Government sets for these sectors will imply the need for early planning and ability to comply by all parties, particularly the construction and ICT sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share what and how are the green procurement criteria decided for these sectors?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Inevitably, there are many requests and requirements when new frameworks are introduced that will effect changes to the traditional industrial practices and processes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: SMEs throughout the world face the same challenges in learning the state of things for sustainability, how to comply with new regulations and where to find essential information that enables necessary compliance, and how to build their business processes and models around sustainability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The issue here is beyond carbon tax or GHGs emissions for any SME.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The crux of managing the issue is knowing where to begin.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Apart from cost, SMEs struggle to implement needful processes and require handholding from understanding the current gaps in their company, and the next steps that are critical for them to becoming a sustainable supplier.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: SMEs need more than just advice or grants, but actually, a 101 guidebook.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many corporates in Singapore rely on local SMEs to fulfil their procurement needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We want to help them and support their transition towards sustainability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But corporates alone will not make the cut for levelling their capabilities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What will the Government do to assist them in reaching the first milestone of understanding their current position and assess the needs to improve upon?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Is it possible to categorise the assessment of SMEs and their needs by nature of businesses, ranging from trading, manufacturing, consumer sales or others.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These would then allow impactful first steps that can give a sense of the state of things in the SMEs and, subsequently, the Government can consider to provide useful targeted support accordingly to them as they transition over time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 must be a whole-of-nation effort that must involve businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In Budget 2023, Minister Grace Fu said that "businesses should do more with less".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Minister also said that while some upfront costs may be incurred, lower energy and resource used will lower costs over the long run.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In a 2023 survey of businesses that have adopted technology to make the green transition, only 16% were confident of achieving their sustainability target.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Businesses are optimistic about the green economy, but may lack the guidance needed to take concrete steps to transition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Beyond making funds available, can the Government proactively reach out to SMEs on accessing and utilising these funds?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope we can provide more support to SMEs to cross the barrier and translate funding into concrete actions on the ground.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's green transition requires all stakeholders to play their part in reducing their carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Enterprises can contribute in many ways, such as by becoming more energy-efficient and reducing waste.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What is the Ministry doing to incentivise businesses to use renewable energy and to reduce energy consumption?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In view of current and new regulations to reduce waste and boost recycling, how is the Ministry supporting companies to build their capabilities to do so?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In addition, are there industry guidelines and targets to encourage business-client cooperation in reducing waste, particularly packaging waste for consumer products?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The higher carbon tax rates will prompt businesses to consider and search for ways to be more energy efficient.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, reasons such as sunk investment cost in current equipment and tools and manpower constraints, especially for SMEs, are some of obstacles for enterprises.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the help and supporting measures available for businesses seeking to be more energy efficient?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's carbon tax has jumped fivefold from $5 per tonne of emissions to $25 per tonne.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the next three years, it will rise to $45 per tonne.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does MSE have to educate, encourage and assist our households to switch to more energy-efficient appliances and adopt green lifestyle habits to obtain savings on their electricity bills?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more hot days and warm nights due to global warming, how can households keep cool without turning to air-conditioning, which is one of the major appliances that consume more electricity?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, in view of the raised carbon tax and our residents' cost of living concerns, how has MSE been helping households to improve their energy and water usage efficiency in order to enhance their cost savings?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How has MSE been working to raise public awareness on tips to conserve these precious resources?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How else can MSE incentivise households that keep water and electricity consumption below national average or certain benchmark consumption per pax to encourage conservation of these resources?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope MSE can share its ongoing and prospective efforts for the points I have raised above.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Singapore's green transition should be a just and inclusive one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am glad that the Climate Friendly Households Programme helps 1-, 2- and 3-room HDB households reduce their energy and water consumption.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The programme gives eligible households vouchers to purchase refrigerators, shower fittings and LED lights.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The programme will expire on 20 March 2024.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry share if there are plans to extend the programme?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Additionally, will the Ministry consider expanding the scope of the programme to include more households and more appliances?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In particular, can we consider expanding the programme to encourage passive cooling measures for households, such as installing heat-reflecting windows and adding insulation to windows and doors?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The National Environment Agency (NEA) currently requires building owners to comply with a set of guidelines to ensure a reasonable standard of indoor air quality and improving ventilation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question that arises is: how will NEA be able to regulate this requirement?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should not wait until the occupants get sick before any investigation is launched on the adequacy of the measures put in place by building owners.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, from a regulatory perspective, how does NEA proactively monitor the owners' compliance of air quality standards in public and commercial buildings?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the compulsory installation of monitors, such as carbon dioxide monitors, in these buildings help in the task?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Carrie Tan, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has had Clean and Green Campaigns since 1990 and most of us recognise the "3Rs" – reduce, reuse and recycle.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But our actions do not mirror this awareness.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Despite much effort, there has been limited success after many years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the domestic recycling rate even dropped slightly in 2022.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is time to shift focus to "reducing" and "reusing" instead, while "recycling" happens in parallel.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Research shows it is the effort required and not the lack of desire that is the obstacle to an action.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When we do not know how to repair, repurpose or reshare an item, discarding it is far easier.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Convenient opportunities to swap and repair items should be permanent features in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, we have successfully run "Shwap for Sustainability" events where residents can exchange clothes with one another to reduce fast fashion waste.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The community group, Repair Kopitiam, organises regular community events in different neighbourhoods where residents can learn how to repair items from trained volunteers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These are two examples of local initiatives that I hope MSE can give resourcing and legs to, to propagate into all neighbourhoods in Singapore through the SG Partnerships Office.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Let us discard the "throw away" mindset and embrace a "treasuring" mindset – using less, sharing more and wasting not.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Let us make reducing and reusing a national movement.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are more people dying each day, each year.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This may sound morbid, but it is the harsh reality and trend going forward.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Do we cut down more trees to make way for more columbariums?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Or can MSE work with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), for example, on research and development to treat ashes to make them beneficial for trees instead?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What are other options to having an urn, a niche and more columbariums for memorialising our loved ones who passed?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge MSE to do more to increase Singaporeans' awareness and willingness towards alternatives, such as inland or sea scattering of ashes.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These conversations need to start now with my generation of millennials, who are more open-minded than our parents and may well opt for alternatives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With an ageing population, rising costs and manpower shortages, there has been concerns over its sustainability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: NEA has implemented programmes and initiatives to support and encourage hawkerprenuers to join the trade.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But, anecdotally, the failure rates of new stalls in some hawker centres and coffee shops has been quite high, with a number of stalls shutting down in less than one year.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Further, many younger hawkerpreneurs aspire to serve more upmarket fare or "atas" fares, such as gourmet pastas, gourmet burgers that start north of $8 in our hawker centres that cater to the taste of more affluent broader population.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Hawkerpreneurs who have the ambition to expand express frustration in the lack of manpower and the inability to hire foreigners as their number one challenge.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What more can the Government do to ensure that the hawker trade can attract and retain Singaporeans, while ensuring the continued availability of good low-cost options in our hawker centres and coffee shops?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Hawker centres are an integral part of our community lives, providing a wide range of good food.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: However, with rising costs of ingredients, manpower and utilities, our hawkers are finding it harder to keep their food prices as affordable as in the past.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: On the other hand, fewer Singaporeans are becoming hawkers, even as many of the current hawkers are getting older and gradually retiring.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What is the Ministry's strategy to maintain the balance between keeping hawker food prices affordable while ensuring the earnings of our hawkers are attractive enough to continue working and to bring in new talent into this sector?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Last year, my Sengkang colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, elucidated that pricey coffee shop rents form part of the recipe for expensive hawker food.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Likewise, hawkers operating from hawker centres face significant pressures from high and rising rents, causing them much financial strain and, inevitably, many may have to raise their food prices, albeit grudgingly, for many well-meaning hawkers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: These pricier rents could likely be due to the operator passing through the high-bids placed during a tender, such as a successful bid of over $6 million for the operation of the recently opened Buangkok Hawker Centre, onto stallholders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Hence, by bringing all centres under NEA control, the costs for our stallholders could be better managed or even reduced, whilst keeping menu prices affordable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: With the introduction of a rental cap for this year's Geylang Serai Ramadan Bazaar, perhaps a similar idea could be implemented for stalls in NEA-operated hawker centres or even other Government-leased properties, such as HDB eating houses as well, instead of a purely price-based tender where hawker stalls are simply awarded to the highest bidder.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: With the rising costs of living hitting Singaporeans hard, measures ought to be in place to ameliorate the financial pressures experienced by hawkers whilst ensuring the affordability of hawker food for all.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, we proudly commemorate Singapore's hawker culture as the nation's inclusion on the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization's (UNESCO's) Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2020.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The dedication of our hawkerpreneurs, who tirelessly work over hot stoves and woks, ensures the preservation of this invaluable cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, our hawkerpreneurs fulfill a crucial social need by providing affordable and delicious meals to all Singaporeans, particularly those from resource-low families.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They also offer convenience to dual-income households, who often lack the time to prepare meals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is worth noting that hawkerpreneurs are restricted from hiring foreign workers, limiting their pool of available stall assistants; two, increased ingredient costs due to global inflation; and three, hawkerpreneurs plying their trade in some coffee shops have also experienced escalating rental prices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Specifically, a study focusing on younger hawkerpreneurs who face higher living expenses, such as housing mortgages and children's education, would be beneficial.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What plans does the Ministry have to ensure that our hawkerpreneurs can maintain a decent livelihood?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, while the Government has emphasised the necessity for consumers to pay more to support the uplifting of lower-wage workers and strengthen social inclusivity, hawkerpreneurs often face criticism when revising meal prices upward.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does the Government intend to assist hawkerpreneurs in implementing price increases that are fair to both them and consumers?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The study concluded that whilst there have been improvements at the hawker centres compared to 2020, Singaporeans conveyed that more should be done to improve toilet sanitation at coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In HDB housing estates, we often see irresponsible cases of littering and dumping among residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They expect the poor Town Council cleaners, who already have heavy workloads, to clean after them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For a first-world country like Singapore, we can certainly do better.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: How do we ingrain in Singaporeans the message that cleanliness is a joint responsibility among all of us?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: How can we improve the cleanliness outcomes in our estates and public toilets?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, cleanliness, or the lack of, in the toilets of our coffee shops and hawker centres has been a perennial issue.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: For a brief period during the COVID-19 pandemic, they improved greatly and Singaporeans were hopeful that finally, clean toilets in our beloved hawker centres will become the new norm.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Unfortunately, this turned out not to be the case, and the state of wet and dirty toilets resumed.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: As a developed country, this is an area in which we must make more effort to improve upon.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What are the plans by the Ministry to address the issue of dirty toilets in public places, including those in the wet markets and coffee shops?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In addition, how can we involve more Singaporeans to keep other public spaces clean?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Recent surveys have shown that the standard of cleanliness in our public toilets at hawker centres and coffeeshops remains disappointing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What plans does the Ministry have to address the longstanding issue of dirty toilets in these public places?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What measures will the Government implement to educate and involve our community to keep our public spaces clean?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Why are public toilets in Singapore in such bad condition, or at least perceived to be?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Could it be because, one, public toilets are not well designed for robust public use, operations and maintenance?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Two, public toilet operators or their contractors are not maintaining toilets to attain and maintain good functional and hygiene standards?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Three, users of public toilets lack graciousness in keeping toilets clean?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Or four, there is a sense of a lack of ownership among all stakeholders to ensure that toilets are functional, safe and clean in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Clean public toilets is certainly not a myth.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: With an ageing population and risks of disease outbreaks in the future, it is crucial for us to ensure that Singapore has clean and hygienic toilets.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Thus, I ask: what plans does MSE have to address the issue of dirty toilets in these public spaces?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: What were the learning points from campaigns that were rolled out in the past?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Do the relevant authorities plan to step up monitoring and enforcement to ensure public toilets are well maintained?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chairman, one of the things we are most known for is being one of the cleanest cities in the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: It is a blessing to be able to walk down litter-free roads built through public culture and awareness and the hard work of many.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And what resources have been deployed to manage errant dumping and high-rise littering, which are sometimes caused by well-meaning elderly who throw food out the window for birds?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What are the Government's strategies to manage to improper waste disposal, particularly at residential HDB units and in our housing estates?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Could MSE also share its strategies working together with other agencies to tackle urban bird issues which persist in several hawker centres and estates?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: “Killer litter” is a term coined decades ago and, today, it continues to be relevant to every one of us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Most of us live in high-rise apartments, whether they are HDB flats or private condominiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: As we have experienced, killer litter can occur anywhere, posing a grave danger to all.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Sometimes, high-rise littering are not deliberate acts of throwing items down the building block.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Rather, these are items placed on ledges or open terraces or hung on balconies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: With more extreme weather conditions nowadays, more items are at risk of injuring someone when there are strong winds.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How will the Government deter potential high-rise littering and ensure that residents take precautions with their items in open areas?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Despite numerous efforts by agencies like NEA, Town Councils and others, the state of public cleanliness and hygiene remains much to be desired.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Irresponsible waste dumping, high-rise littering and cigarette butt littering remain a common scene in our neighbourhoods and heartland centres.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While the majority of the public are socially responsible, there are still a recalcitrant minority that continues to be inconsiderate and behave irresponsibly.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It seems that the effect of deterrence has no impact on them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chairman, foreigners and tourists often speak of Singapore as a clean city-state.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a reputation we want to maintain.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We also want to ensure our residents live well in a clean and healthy environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have been able to achieve this so far due to the hard work of our cleaners.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are also meaningful initiatives, like the ones led by our Public Hygiene Council.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, as locals, we know there are some challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Indeed, it can be difficult to keep certain places, like public toilets in hawker centres, clean.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to create a culture where people take responsibility and participate in the efforts of maintaining hygiene and cleanliness, so that we can truly be a clean city and not a "cleaned" one.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need a whole-of-society approach in tackling this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How is MSE working with different agencies and community partners in this endeavour?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also note that NUS and JTC Corporation are supporting trials with autonomous cleaning bots in toilets at industrial parks, hospitals, malls and the airport.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How can the Government leverage technological advancements in managing hotspots where cleanliness is an issue?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Designated smoking areas are created to confine smokers and their smoke within a space and protect non-smokers from the harmful effects of second-hand tobacco smoke.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Without these clearly designated zones, smokers are more likely to break the law and smoke in a prohibited area.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister what is the progress of designating smoking areas in buildings, F&B outlets and various other spaces, and if there are plans to expand their set-ups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have been pushing the issue of second-hand smoke repeatedly for the past few years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We cannot end the MSE Committee of Supply (COS) without including this important issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I know Senior Minister of State Amy Khor has reluctantly handed over this issue to Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope with a fresh pair of eyes and his healthy lungs – he exercises a lot – we can finally move forward on this issue of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is ironic that we are doing so much to protect public health, implement measures to reduce pollution levels and improve air quality but we do so little when it comes to protecting people from second-hand smoke in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But for so many people, second-hand smoke is a deadly intruder.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This should not be treated as a neighbourly dispute but instead, treated as a public health concern.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have given many suggestions to tackle second-hand smoke in homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Beyond issuing advisories, can the Government share what it is doing to protect people from second-hand smoke in their own homes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Next, since 2019, Orchard Road has been designated a "No Smoking Zone".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This means that smoking is only allowed in designated smoking areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It has been five years since we introduced the Orchard Road "No Smoking Zone".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on its assessment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Ministry consider expanding the "No Smoking Zone" to other busy streets and areas, such as the Central Business District and the Civic District?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In our early days of Independence, Singapore stood at critical crossroads, with limited resources, an uncertain economic future and pressing public health concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Back then, our forefathers recognised the importance of safeguarding a clean and green environment to protect the health of our people, fuel economic growth and pave the way for a brighter future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A public cleaning regime was put in place, where our cleaning workforce swept the streets and removed refuse daily.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We cleaned up the Singapore River, which was heavily polluted from human and economic activities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Street hawkers were rehoused into hawker centres, equipped with proper facilities to ensure food safety and hygiene standards.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Today, we again stand at crossroads of political, economic, social and environmental changes.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is why the Government launched the Forward Singapore exercise last year, to re-examine our values and aspirations, and to forge a new social compact for the road ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Forward SG underscored the crucial role of collective responsibility in shaping our shared future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It also highlighted the importance of ensuring that the basic needs of all Singaporeans continue to be met.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This includes a clean and liveable environment, with reliable access to safe food and water.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: My Ministry will work with all segments of our society to build a clean, green and resilient home for our current and future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In this COS debate, I will provide an overview of our efforts to enhance public hygiene and update on the Singapore Green Plan; Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will talk about our efforts in green procurement, energy efficiency and waste management; Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will speak about how we are enhancing our food security, protecting our coasts and strengthening the resilience of our hawkers; and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will delve into the operational and technological aspects of our environmental cleanliness initiatives, as well as our community engagement efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What comes to mind is environmental cleanliness, keeping our surroundings free from litter and clutter and the iconic “Keep Singapore Clean” campaign.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It forms the very foundation of our well-being – safe food, clean air and clean water.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Collectively, all facets of public hygiene come together to create a thriving urban environment and protect our physical and mental health.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Sustaining high levels of public hygiene requires the active participation of all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government, businesses, communities and individuals must all work together to contribute to a clean environment, safe food, clean air and clean water.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is the social compact that will strengthen our sense of collective responsibility to one another.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Complementing enforcement are our efforts to harness the spirit of collective responsibility as part of Forward SG, for all stakeholders to play a role in upkeeping good public hygiene practices for the betterment of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey will elaborate on this.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government has been working closely with our businesses to keep our public spaces clean.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It also requires premises to appoint a trained and registered individual to develop and implement an ES programme in accordance with prescribed standards.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our agencies have been working diligently with business owners to ensure that minimum cleanliness standards set out under the ES regime and others under the EPHA are met.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several Members – Ms Poh Li San, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Murali Pillai – have raised questions on toilets in coffeeshops and other public spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NEA and SFA have been conducting enforcement blitzes on public toilets, including those in coffee shops and hawker centres, to ensure that they are properly maintained and cleaned according to requirements under the EPHA.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NEA and SFA have also been conducting checks to ensure proper disposal of food waste by food establishments, to provide clean, pest-free dining environments for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This includes making sure that establishments have sufficient and properly maintained bins, and that any waste generated is properly bagged, conveyed to the bin centre in a timely manner, and not left overnight.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will step up on enforcement where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey will speak more on our approach.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, our cleaning industry has been a cornerstone of our environmental cleanliness efforts, forming the backbone of our clean-up initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With an ageing population and a shrinking workforce, the industry faces shortages and reductions in manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is important for us to uplift our cleaning industry, to ensure that they are adequately equipped and resourced to uphold high standards of environmental cleanliness.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have seen several efforts, led by the industry, in supporting our cleaning workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Temasek Polytechnic launched their Enviro Tech Innovation Hub (ETIH) last year, with the support of NEA, together with the Environmental Management Association of Singapore and industry players, such as cleaning companies and tech partners.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The ETIH will develop training programmes to upskill our cleaning industry and testbed cutting-edge technology solutions to increase productivity, such as the usage of IoT sensors and devices to manage cleanliness performance.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are actively upskilling our cleaners, so that their capabilities and skillsets evolve in tandem with the industry’s needs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We introduced enhanced training requirements under the PWM for the cleaning industry in December 2022, which has allowed cleaners to acquire new and relevant skills, such as how to operate emerging technologies and digitalisation tools used in cleaning operations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: SFA takes a risk-based approach in regulating food safety, where licensing requirements and food safety grading criteria are calibrated based on food establishments’ risk profiles.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This focuses our inspection resources on where risks are higher and encourages businesses to implement sufficient measures to ensure food safety, while keeping compliance costs low.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Under the existing grading system, food establishments are graded between A and D, based on an annual audit.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This provides a snapshot of an establishment’s food safety standards at the point of inspection.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, it does not adequately reflect whether these standards are consistently maintained.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For better food safety assurance, we are moving towards a new Safety Assurance for Food Establishments (SAFE) framework, where establishments will be graded based on their food safety track record and prevailing food safety management systems.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It will also harmonise the grading systems for both retail and non-retail food establishments, which are currently regulated by two different frameworks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In line with our risk-based approach, establishments involved in significant food handling with a large scale of distribution, such as food manufacturers and caterers, will need to meet additional requirements to attain higher grades compared to those of smaller scale.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Establishments with poor food safety performance and lower grades will face more frequent inspection.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Poor performance during these inspections could lead to downgrading.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This new SAFE Framework is a better version from the one we announced in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: SFA incorporated the feedback it has received from the industry and kept the intent of recognising food establishments with a consistent record of good food safety performance, and spurring others to achieve and maintaining high grades of food safety.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More details will be released later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With a risk-based approach, we are also removing licensing requirements and fees on food establishments with minimal food safety risk.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More than half of existing market stall licensees and around two in five existing vending machine licensees will benefit from this new policy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The safety of food from these stalls and vending machines will continue to be regulated through standards imposed by SFA on the importers and suppliers of these food items.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Another aspect of public hygiene is the quality of indoor air which Mr Pillai spoke about.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Formaldehyde is a chemical that can be found in some building products, such as paints.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Prolonged exposure to formaldehyde can lead to negative health effects, such as respiratory discomfort and an increased risk of certain cancers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To protect our people from such exposure, we will be progressively introducing limits on formaldehyde in building products, starting with interior paints.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To Mr Pillai’s question on how we are safeguarding indoor air quality in buildings, NEA currently does not mandate minimum indoor air quality standards for buildings.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Instead, NEA takes the approach of promoting greater business responsibility in maintaining high levels of indoor air quality and providing guidance on best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NEA, the Building Construction Authority (BCA) and the Ministry of Health (MOH) have jointly issued a set of guidelines on improving ventilation and indoor air quality in buildings, which Mr Pillai had mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These guidelines encourage premises managers to install carbon dioxide monitors to assess the adequacy of ventilation in their premises.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NEA has also published a detailed guide for premises managers on how to implement carbon dioxide monitoring.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Pillai also asked for an update on the implementation of the Code of Practice (COP) for the Control of Legionella Bacteria in Cooling Towers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The COP was replaced by the Code of Practice for Environmental Health (COPEH) and related Guidelines in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Under the EPHA, we require all cooling towers to be registered with NEA to enhance the traceability and control of potential outbreaks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ensuring a supply of clean water is a collective responsibility shared by both the Government and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Businesses must play an active role by implementing adequate earth control measures to prevent silt from being washed into our waterways and reservoirs, and refrain from disposing hazardous substances into our public sewerage system.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On the Government’s part, the Public Utilities Board (PUB) will look to introduce additional measures to safeguard our waterways, reservoirs and sewerage system.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This includes tightening controls on silt discharges into our waterways and reservoirs, and illegal discharges of dangerous and hazardous substances into our public sewerage system.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Chairman, even as we draw focus on the "hygiene" factors in the year ahead, we are not taking our eyes off longer-term challenges, such as climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Ms Poh Li San asked for an update on the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are making good progress to achieve our targets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Dr Lim asked about the progress of specific initiatives and targets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I will not go into details of each target under the Green Plan but focus on providing an overview of our key achievements.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I invite Dr Lim to separately file questions on specific initiatives and targets to the respective Green Plan Ministries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On "City in Nature", the Ministry of National Development (MND) and the National Parks Board (NParks) are pressing on with conserving and extending our natural capital throughout the island.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will provide further details during MND’s COS.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On "Sustainable Living", my Ministry rolled out the Disposable Carrier Bag Charge last year, requiring large supermarket operators to charge for disposable carrier bags.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More Singaporeans are observed to use reusable carrier bags for their grocery shopping.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) has also been instilling sustainable living habits in our students through the Eco Stewardship Programme, where schools have implemented the "4Cs" approach of curriculum, campus, culture and community to allow students to learn about sustainability in a more integrated and applied manner.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are also powering on with our "Energy Reset".

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To foster an inclusive transition to a green economy, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced Greenprint, a digital solution to help businesses simplify and standardise the reporting of sustainability data.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Greenprint will launch in phases in 2024 and focus initially on automating basic climate reporting for SMEs, before scaling its automation capabilities to support larger corporates.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To secure our "Resilient Future", my Ministry is pressing on with our efforts to ensure that our environment remains liveable, our food supply remains reliable and our coastlines remain well-protected in the face of extreme weather patterns.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister of State Khor recently updated this House on the measures we are taking to increase Singapore’s heat resilience, which should address Ms Poh’s queries on the topic.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh will update on our food security and coastal protection efforts later.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Dr Lim alluded to, the Green Plan is a living plan that will evolve over time with more ambitious targets and aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In 2022, we announced that the public sector will commit to achieve net zero emissions around 2045.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Last year, we raised our target for restoration and enhancement of forest, coastal and marine habitats from 30 hectares to 80 hectares by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are closely monitoring the progress of our initiatives to ensure that they remain relevant to our long-term sustainability goals.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, as the world grapples with daunting, long-term challenges like climate change, let us not lose sight of the fundamental necessities for a good and healthy life – a clean environment, safe food, clean air and clean water.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As committed under Forward SG, the Government will continue to spearhead efforts towards our shared vision of a clean, green and resilient Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But we can do so only through collective action with our businesses and our people.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: My hope is for Singapore to be a clean country and not just a cleaned country, and I echo the comment made by Ms Rahayu Mahzam.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I hope to see businesses operate with pride, offering not only clean spaces for Singaporeans, but also implementing responsible practices that safeguard the food we eat, the air we breathe, and the water we drink.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I hope to see communities become engines of positive change, fostering a culture of shared ownership and partnering the Government in building a new social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I hope to see Singaporeans treat our streets, our parks and our public spaces like extensions of our own homes, going the extra mile to keep our surroundings clean as Singapore is our home.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is the Singapore we deserve, the Singapore we can build, and the Singapore we must leave for generations to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, while we push hard on public hygiene, which is the foundation for healthy, resilient communities, we must also press on with our efforts to confront climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Climate change has profound impacts on public hygiene and public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have taken concrete steps to reduce our carbon footprint.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These include gradually increasing our carbon tax rate, facilitating renewable energy imports and promoting energy efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Everyone needs to fight climate change – the Government, businesses and households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In 2021, we launched GreenGov.SG, the public sector's sustainability movement, where we committed to ambitious carbon and resource efficiency targets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Last December, we published the inaugural GreenGov.SG report, which documented our sustainability efforts, progress and plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan and Mr Don Wee asked about our plans for the next GreenGov.SG report and whether Scope 3 emissions would be included.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The second report will be released this year and will include data on waste and waste reduction efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As there are wide-ranging sources of Scope 3 emissions from the Government's extensive activities and the sources that are deemed material vary across agencies, we are still studying the appropriate approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Under GreenGov.SG, we are pursuing green Government procurement to spur more environmentally sustainable business practices and accelerate the supply of more environmentally friendly goods and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We want to encourage companies to green their processes and products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As announced at COS last year, we will consider the sustainability practices of companies that tender for Government projects, starting with large construction and ICT projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is on top of the sustainability requirements that we have imposed for the goods we procure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Miss Chan and Mr Wee also asked how we decided on the green Government procurement criteria for the construction and ICT sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Over the past year, we have consulted the industry and incorporated their feedback on the environmental sustainability-related evaluation criteria.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Subsequently, we piloted the criteria by setting aside up to 5% of evaluation points for five construction tenders and one ICT bulk tender.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For the pilot construction tenders, companies were assessed on whether they have carried out climate-related disclosures; adopted decarbonisation technologies, such as electric generators; incorporated low-carbon construction materials; and achieved relevant sustainability certifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For the ICT sector, hardware suppliers were assessed based on criteria, such as sustainable packaging options and sustainability-related certifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also plan to include criteria for data centre operators and cloud service providers, such as whether companies have embarked on sustainability reporting and the power usage effectiveness of their data centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to refine our environmental sustainability evaluation criteria for large construction and ICT tenders with minimum estimated procurement value of $50 million and $10 million respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To Mr Wee's query on the expansion timeline, we plan to expand this initiative to include companies that tender for meetings, incentives, conferences, and exhibitions (MICE) and other events organised by the public sector from FY2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will conduct industry consultations with key players, before finalising the details.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Beyond the public sector, we will continue to facilitate the greening of businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We hope to encourage companies, particularly SMEs who are less well-resourced, to adopt sustainability practices while improving their bottom line.
